title: Fragility persists when weak institutions, repeated shocks, fiscal constraint, and human-capital loss reinforce one another
source_unit: World Bank, Fragile and Conflict-Affected Situations: Intertwined Crises, Multiple Vulnerabilities
geography: Economies classified as fragile and conflict-affected situations, with comparisons to other developing countries and global poverty, health, education, food, debt, and growth outcomes

observations.period: 2026; persistence and overlapping shocks in fragile and conflict-affected situations

denominator.unit: World Bank FCS economy classification and vulnerability frame

long_term_classification.unit: approximate percent of FCS economies remaining classified as such for more than a decade

institutional_condition.value: weak institutions constrain responses to conflict, natural disasters, commodity-price swings, and global downturns

fiscal_constraint.value: limited fiscal space constrains investment in education, health, infrastructure, and shock response

policy_route.value: state capacity, governance, tailored policy, and sustained international support are identified as routes to resilience

observations.method: World Bank comparative analysis of fragile and conflict-affected situations, institutional conditions, overlapping shocks, fiscal capacity, and development outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: Classification is an analytical and operational construct; persistence does not imply that every institution or community within an FCS economy is equally fragile.
observations.subgroup: FCS governments, households, firms, local institutions, conflict-affected communities, and populations exposed to overlapping shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Long classification duration can coexist with institutional reform, local resilience, or improved outcomes in particular sectors and places.

observations.period: early 2000s-2026; conflict frequency, lethality, and economic scarring

denominator.unit: World Bank five-year conflict and post-conflict growth comparison frame

conflict_change.value: on a five-year basis, the frequency and lethality of conflicts have more than tripled since the early 2000s

gdp_per_capita_scarring.unit: approximate cumulative percent GDP-per-capita drop after five years following high-intensity conflict relative to pre-conflict projections

shock_transmission.value: conflict produces human and economic losses while interacting with natural disasters, commodity swings, and global downturns

recovery_boundary.value: post-conflict recovery is not automatic and depends on institutions, policy, financing, and peace conditions

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of conflict trends and comparative post-conflict GDP-per-capita trajectories relative to pre-conflict projections.
observations.uncertainty: The GDP estimate is a comparative macroeconomic estimate, not a realized loss for every household or a causal forecast independent of conflict intensity, duration, policy, and external support.
observations.subgroup: Conflict-affected households, workers, firms, public institutions, displaced populations, and communities rebuilding infrastructure and services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some economies recover faster than the aggregate pattern through peace agreements, institutional rebuilding, external support, and diversified production.

observations.period: 2024-2030; poverty, extreme poverty, and acute food insecurity in FCS economies

denominator.unit: FCS population and global extreme-poverty projection frame

extreme_poverty_share.unit: percent of the population of FCS economies living in extreme poverty

global_extreme_poor_2030.unit: projected percent of the world's extreme poor living in FCS economies by 2030

global_extreme_poor_2024.unit: percent of the world's extreme poor living in FCS economies in 2024

acute_food_insecurity.unit: people in FCS economies facing acute food insecurity

food_share.unit: approximate share of the FCS population facing acute food insecurity

observations.method: World Bank poverty, food-security, and fragility synthesis using FCS economy estimates and global extreme-poverty projections.
observations.uncertainty: Poverty and food-security estimates differ in reference years, thresholds, coverage, and conflict-related data availability; projections are not fixed outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Poor households, people in conflict-affected and hunger-prone areas, children, displaced populations, farmers, and humanitarian systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Peace, governance, social protection, markets, and targeted assistance can change poverty and food-security trajectories; the projection highlights risk, not inevitability.

observations.period: 2026; health, education, and debt vulnerability in FCS economies

denominator.unit: FCS human-capital and debt-vulnerability comparison frame

life_expectancy_gap.unit: years shorter life expectancy in FCS economies than in other developing countries

infant_mortality.unit: more-than-fold infant-mortality rate in FCS economies compared with other developing countries

schooling.unit: average years of schooling received by children in FCS economies

debt_distress.unit: percent of FCS economies in or at high risk of debt distress

service_strain.value: health systems are under severe strain and education and infrastructure are disrupted by conflict and fiscal constraint

observations.method: World Bank comparison of FCS human-capital outcomes, health-system strain, education, and debt-vulnerability indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Aggregate gaps do not identify individual treatment, schooling, or debt outcomes and may reflect selection, conflict exposure, geography, and data limitations.
observations.subgroup: Children, women, patients, students, indebted governments, public-service workers, and households experiencing disrupted health and education.
observations.counterinterpretation: Targeted health, education, infrastructure, debt, and governance investments can improve outcomes even under fragility; FCS populations are not defined only by deficits.

related_sources.claim: World Bank FY2027 FCV classifications distinguish public conflict prevalence from institutional fragility.
World Bank FCV strategy provides complementary operational and state-capacity context.

boundary: This record adds a fragility-to-poverty and state-capacity route across persistent classification, overlapping shocks, conflict scarring, poverty, food insecurity, health, education, infrastructure, and debt. It uses aggregate World Bank analysis, not household respondent histories, individual health or schooling records, local case files, causal conflict forecasts, or proof that every FCS economy follows the same pathway.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank FCS publication page reviewed for persistence, overlapping shocks, conflict trends, GDP scarring, extreme poverty, food insecurity, health, education, debt distress, and policy response findings.
